overview:
Before dawn on 24 February 2022, Russian forces crossed into Ukraine along four broad axes at once: south from Belarus toward Kyiv, north from occupied Crimea, west from the Donbas territories held by Russian-backed separatists since 2014, and across the eastern border toward Kharkiv and Sumy. Vladimir Putin framed it as an operation to "demilitarise and denazify" a neighbouring state, and much of the initial plan assumed the government in Kyiv would collapse within days. Airborne troops seized Antonov Airport at Hostomel on the first morning to open an air bridge into the capital; other columns took the Chernobyl exclusion zone, invested Chernihiv and Sumy, and captured the small Black Sea outcrop of Snake Island. The capital did not fall. Ukrainian defenders held the approaches through Irpin, Bucha and Vasylkiv, Western anti-tank and anti-air weapons bled the long Russian supply columns, and by late March and early April Russian forces withdrew from the whole northern front. Kherson, taken on 2 March, remained the only regional capital Russia captured in the opening campaign.

What the retreat from the north uncovered shaped how much of the world read the war afterwards. In Bucha and dozens of other settlements around Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kharkiv and Sumy, UN human rights monitors documented summary executions of civilians — over 300 in the first months alone, with hundreds of bodies recovered in Bucha itself — alongside torture, arbitrary detention and conflict-related sexual violence. Russia denied responsibility and called the evidence staged; independent investigators, the UN Commission of Inquiry and the International Criminal Court concluded otherwise. Meanwhile the fighting shifted east and south: the port of Mariupol was reduced and taken after a siege of nearly three months, a missile struck the railway station at Kramatorsk while evacuees waited on the platforms, and long-range strikes on the electricity grid became a standing feature of the autumn and winter. In September Ukraine broke the Russian line east of Kharkiv in a matter of days, retaking Izium and Kupiansk; in November Russia abandoned Kherson city and pulled back across the Dnipro. Between those two reversals Moscow staged referendums and declared the annexation of four oblasts it did not fully control, and mobilised several hundred thousand additional men.

The war reordered a great deal beyond the front line. Millions of Ukrainians left the country, in the largest refugee movement in Europe since the Second World War, and millions more were displaced inside it. Western states imposed sanctions of unprecedented scope on Russian finance, energy and technology, froze central bank reserves, and moved from supplying man-portable weapons to artillery, HIMARS rocket systems and air defence. Finland and Sweden applied to join NATO, the alliance Russia had demanded stop enlarging. Nuclear risk hung over everything: Russian troops held the Zaporizhzhia plant, and Putin's periodic hints about strategic weapons were taken seriously enough to shape Western decisions about which arms to send. When a missile fell in Przewodów in Poland in November, killing two, the first fear was of an Article 5 moment; investigators concluded it was most likely a Ukrainian air-defence interceptor gone astray. The year closed with the front roughly frozen around Bakhmut, and no negotiation in sight.
significance: The invasion ended the assumption, thirty years old in Europe, that large-scale interstate conquest was a settled question there. It broke Russia's own reputation for military competence, revived and enlarged NATO, forced Europe off Russian gas at speed, and pushed Ukraine decisively toward the European Union — the opposite of every stated aim. It also became the most closely documented war in history, fought under commercial satellites, smartphones and open-source analysts, which meant atrocities like Bucha entered the evidentiary record within weeks rather than decades and reached the International Criminal Court in the same span. For much of the world outside Europe it registered differently: as a grain and fertiliser shock, an energy price shock, and a test of whether the rules invoked against Russia are applied consistently. The lines drawn in 2022 — the failed dash for Kyiv, the two counteroffensives, the annexation of ground Russia did not hold — still define the shape of the conflict and the terms of any eventual settlement.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, the Council on Foreign Relations conflict tracker, and UN human rights reporting on the first months of the invasion; the dataset's 71 events cluster heavily on the northern campaign of February–April 2022 and thin out badly for the Donbas and southern fighting, where Mariupol, Sievierodonetsk and Bakhmut belong. Casualty figures are the weakest part of the record: military losses on both sides are state secrets and the published estimates diverge by an order of magnitude, verified civilian death tolls are acknowledged undercounts, and the toll in Mariupol and other occupied cities remains unknown. Russian accounts of events such as Bucha are official denials rather than an independent counter-record, and reporting from occupied territory is severely restricted.
